meaningMnemonic: What's under the lid on your cook pot? Legs and fins. Again . All you know how to cook is legs (of chicken) and fins, so you cook them again and again and again. You'll be having them for dinner tonight, and again tomorrow, and again the next day. Legs and fins, again and again and again, for the rest of your days. Alternatively, you can also think of this as a laundry hanger with a pair of pants and two little socks flapping like fins. Because laundry is something you have to do again and again… whether you like it or not!

This is the broom radical, because the top part looks like a sideways hand broom and the bottom part looks like a dustpan. Alternatively, you can remember this one with its components: Wolverine wipes his forehead with a towel every time he picks up a broom, because sweeping gets him sweaty fast. Poor guy can fight supervillains all day, but give him a broom and he's instantly exhausted.
When a mama watches over a man, it gives him the courage he needs to take on any foe.

Don't confuse this with triceratops. Grass is closer together, and a little bushier, like this. It's also more random and squished down in parts. If you see a bush of lines like this, it's probably going to be grass.

You see a narwhal struggling with a measuring tape, trying to measure his height ! His fins can't reach the end of the tape, but of course he wants to include his glorious tusk. Measuring height is not an easy tusk… er, task for a narwhal, but he'll figure it out. Probably.
In prison, your mouth is not allowed to talk freely. Get a piece of paper to use in place of your mouth and start writing your thoughts out in paragraph form!
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means past .
A creeper in a rice paddy? That's just a scarecrow !
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means walk .

The thread you weave together to tell others about oneself is the account of your life. It's your very own narrative , tying everything you've been through together. Hints Picture this account of your life, the thread of the narrative linking all of the different important points in your life together.
readingMnemonic: You take this account and lock it with a special key ( き ). You only give this key to people you really trust, so they can read the account of your life and truly understand you. Hints Picture the people in your life that you'd give this special key to. They'd get to read the account of your life, so make sure they're trustworthy before you hand that key over.

meaningMnemonic: You run into someone's forehead with your car . The big forehead you hit is Kim Jong Un's. You know that now you're going to have the whole North Korean army coming after you. Hints Imagine yourself running away from the North Korean army. You have to get to the border, the entire army is coming after you for hitting their dear leader!
readingMnemonic: The army is after you. Each army soldier has a gun ( ぐん ) and they want to use these guns of theirs to shoot you dead! You killed their leader with a car and now they’re gonna get you back with a gun! Hints Picture yourself running away from them as they shout and shoot at you. Hear the bullets wizzing past your head as you run away as fast as you can.

meaningMnemonic: Grain s look like they're on fire in autumn . They all turn red and orange and brown, the colors of fire. It's also fun to set grains on fire in Autumn, since it's getting colder. Hints Picture all the grains in autumn. Picture all of the colors. The colors of fire.
readingMnemonic: As the grains burn, and the season changes to autumn, imagine them yelling out in pain: " ACK ( あき )!" Hints Ah yes, the sound of the seasons changing to autumn. Ack! Ack! Ack!

meaningMnemonic: To your leader , you say : " Believe and trust in me." The leader doesn't think you can handle your duties, so you have to say this to him. You want him to believe and trust that you're responsible. You can handle this task. Hints Imagine who your leader is here — maybe a boss, or maybe the Crabigator. Now say it out loud to this imagined leader: "Believe and trust in me!"
readingMnemonic: As you face your leader and say " Believe and trust in me," you kneel down on each shin ( しん ). You have shin splints, so it hurts a bit, but you do it anyway to show how serious you are. Hints Picture yourself pleading with your leader to trust and believe in you. Imagine the pain from your shin splints as you kneel. It hurts a lot, but it proves how serious you are.

meaningMnemonic: A mountain stone is probably going to be a really big stone. We're talking about a boulder here. Hints This kanji makes a lot of sense. Just follow the logic.
readingMnemonic: " Boulder !!!" yells a voice from behind you. " Eee, wha ...?" ( いわ ) you reply. You look up to see a boulder falling off the cliff above you. "Eeeeee! Whaaaat!?," you shout again, running and screaming this time. Hints Imagine yourself screaming "Eeeeee! Whaaaat!?" and running away from that boulder as fast as you can.

meaningMnemonic: Your leader in private is Buddha . You don't feel the need to tell everyone. But when you're alone you give your time to Buddha and let him lead your life. Hints Imagine being in the privacy of your own home, your own room, and saying to yourself, "Yes, Buddha, you're my leader." Or don't, if that doesn't sit right with you. Freedom of religion and all that, right?
readingMnemonic: Your private Buddha is a little different than other people's idea of him. Your Buddha is wearing boots ( ぶつ ). They're big and rubber, and they look fabulous on him. Hints Picture Buddha wearing a giant pair of rubber boots. Yes, now this is fashion.

meaningMnemonic: If you see an animal among the flowers in a rice paddy , chances are it’s a cat . Cats love rice paddy flowers, almost as much as they love catnip. Hints Picture this cat meowing and purring as it rubs up against all the flowers in the rice paddy field. Aww, it’s so cute!
readingMnemonic: Wait a minute… This cat is pretty odd looking. You take a closer look, seeing it is missing its neck ( ねこ ). You go to pet it, but it's super sensitive about that area of its head, which is basically a face connected to a body... Hints Try not to imagine this too hard. It is disturbing.

meaningMnemonic: Again and again, winter change s you each year. Hints With every winter that comes around, another year passes, and you change. Again and again. The never ending cycle of winters and change.
readingMnemonic: You know what else change s each winter? Hen s ( へん )! They're constantly laying eggs, which then (possibly) turn into new hens. Hints Picture you and your hens. Going through change, every winter, again and again.

meaningMnemonic: The sun is out, the sky is blue , things have begun to clear up ! Hints Look into the blue sky and imagine the clouds parting as the weather clears up and the sun starts to come out. Gorgeous! The beauty is so great you have to squint.
readingMnemonic: When it starts to clear up , you exclaim, " Hah ( は )! Told you so!" You had a feeling it would clear up, but no one believed you, so now you have to yell "Hah!" and rub your correctness in everyone's face. Hints Imagine walking down the street as the weather clears up and saying to everyone you pass, "Hah! I was right! I knew it would clear up! Hah!" Basking in the beautiful weather is nice, but basking in feelings of smug superiority is even better.

meaningMnemonic: The radical for courage and the kanji for courage are exactly the same. Hints That means if you know your radicals well, you know the meaning of this kanji too!
readingMnemonic: A man needs courage to stand up to all the you ths ( ゆう ) of the world. They are so numerous and difficult to understand, but the man can face them with courage thanks to his mama. Hints Imagine a courageous man standing against the youths. They use weird slang and try to tell him about avocado toast, but the man keeps his courage.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami approaches, and anyone who dares to stand in front of it will surely cry . That tsunami is going to hit you hard, and rip you right off the ground you're standing on. Who wouldn't cry? Hints Imagine getting hit with the full force of a tsunami. It slams into you and crushes every bone in your body. It hurts so much you cry.
readingMnemonic: Do you know the only way to stop yourself cry ing after a tsunami? That's right, na chos ( な )! Nachos are the only proven way to cheer people up after being hit by a tsunami. Hints Imagine stuffing yourself with nachos. The tears stop. You're feeling bruised and wet, but much better.

meaningMnemonic: Throw a cape over a creeper , and suddenly they think they're a big-shot director . They go around calling themselves managing director of this, director-general of that. They creep into meetings and ceremonies and try to direct the proceedings, all because of that stupid cape. Hints Picture the creepiest creeper you know. They're wearing a cape, laughing from behind a big desk in their new director-level position. That cape has really gone to their head.
readingMnemonic: After this creeper dons the cape, they decide to become Director of Shee p ( し ). From now on all sheep-related business, government policy, and law will be determined by this creeper in a cape, because they are the Director of Sheep. Hints Picture that creeper you know. Their cape is made of wool now, since they're the Director of Sheep, and they're directing all kinds of creepy policy decisions about sheep. I'm not even sure what those would be, but try to imagine some.

meaningMnemonic: This cage with treasure in it is actually a map of the district the treasure is in. Hints Picture a big pirate map, and on it are a bunch of these markers for the districts where you can find the treasures you've been searching for.
readingMnemonic: There is one district you're interested in, and that's the coo kie ( く ) district. Hints The treasure of the cookie district is cookies, which you want. And to be fair, even if you weren't a pirate, you'd probably want those cookies.

meaningMnemonic: There are many flowers in the center of England . It may seem rainy and gray at first, but if you walk right to the center you'll see all the flowers that grow there in the center of the country. This kanji also means English , which is pretty similar to England. Just imagine all the people of England walking to the center, where the flowers are, and speaking English to them to help them grow. Hints Picture yourself in the center of England, speaking English to all of the beautiful flowers.
readingMnemonic: You keep walking to the very central center of England and see a giant a corn ( えい ) planted in the middle of the ground. This acorn is the source of all the flowers and life in England. Hints Imagine walking around the giant English acorn. Touch its smooth surface with your hand.

meaningMnemonic: The height radical and the height kanji are the same! That said, there's a secondary meaning to this kanji of ten feet . So, when you think of height, think of that height as being ten feet (or three meters ) tall. Hints If you paid attention in radicals school, you'll be able to learn this kanji meaning easily.
readingMnemonic: When you think of height , think of our huge farmhand friend, Joe ( じょう ). He's a big guy, and he has a lot of height to him. In fact, he's ten feet tall. Hints Joe really is a big guy. Look up at him, and try to measure him, although ten feet might be a little high for you to reach.

meaningMnemonic: The husband radical and the husband kanji are the same. How useful, unlike some husbands, I'd imagine.
readingMnemonic: What do all husband s love? Foo d ( ふう )! Can you hear your future husband? He’s saying, "Fooooood! FOOOOOD!” like some kind of food craving zombie. Hints Husbands love eating food. Who doesn’t though, really?

meaningMnemonic: Members of the tongue clan like to do one thing: lick . They go around licking everything to mark their tongue clan territory, you know? They even lick each other on the cheek by way of greeting. Hints Imagine encountering the tongue clan in your travels and being greeted by a whole village of them. It's kinda gross at first, with your cheeks getting all slick from the saliva, but after a while you get used to it.
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately, the tongue clan members also lick your na chos ( な ). You'd been saving those nachos! They were your travel rations. Now each and every nacho has been licked clean. Hints Seems this tongue clan only likes food that can be licked up, like nacho cheese and salsa. They lap up all the good stuff, so all that's left for you are some soggy, pale, naked nachos.

meaningMnemonic: When a spirit decides to live in your scarecrow , you'll be granted good luck and good fortune . Crows won't hang out in your farm. Everything you grow will become large and delicious. But not everyone is so lucky that a spirit will decide to live in their scarecrow. So maybe the luck was in you all along! Hints Nope, the luck is definitely coming from the spirit in your scarecrow. You aren't lucky on your own.
readingMnemonic: You want to check the scarecrow to make sure your recent luck is coming from it, so you kick it. " F*** ( ふく ) you!" it yells. Oh yeah, there's a spirit in there. Hints If you get a luck spirit to say f*** you, you might accidentally convince it to move somewhere else. If it does, you lose your luck. So be careful.

meaningMnemonic: You might want to eat , but your anti -eating stance means your meal will just sit in front of you, uneaten. Food is meant to be eaten! Stop trying to fast and take a bite. Hints Look down at the huge meal in front of you. You'll have to eat your food eventually, but I guess there are plenty of reasons to be anti-eat right now.
readingMnemonic: As you stare at the meal , Han ( はん ) Solo appears before you and takes a bite! This is what happens if you don't eat your food, someone else will eat it. Hints Picture Han Solo slowly eating your whole meal. He's making constant eye contact with you, reaching down and shoving the entire meal into his mouth.

meaningMnemonic: If you want to say how big a cross is, you have to measure it. You can't say the size of something without measuring it first. Hints Imagine trying to use your hands to show the size of this cross, but the other person shakes their head and says, "Use your words!" Ugh, okay, you'll have to measure it then.
readingMnemonic: You need to measure this cross but all you have is a ca ke ( けい ). Good enough! I'm sure all cakes are exactly the same size, so they're a reliable unit of measure. Hints "This cross measures two cakes wide and three cakes long," you say.

meaningMnemonic: Tsunami s in the past changed the method s and law s of today. Hints Tsunamis used to come crashing into towns, just leveling them completely. Today we have new methods of building and protecting ourselves, and laws to keep them in place, so the past doesn't repeat itself.
readingMnemonic: These method s and law s affected your own ho me ( ほう ) the most. Hints Your home has strong walls and ceilings. You aren't allowed to leave the doors unlocked and open. These methods and laws are because of those past tsunamis and the damage they used to cause. Your home is safe thanks to them!

meaningMnemonic: The sun has an excuse for disappearing at night . The sun gets really tired, same as anyone else – so when night rolls around the sun excuses itself and goes to sleep. It’s a valid excuse. Hints Imagine you’re the sun, working all day. Of course you get tired. This is a good excuse to go to bed at night and get some rest. Feel how sore and hot and sweaty and exhausted you are after a hard day’s work of being the sun.
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately, you also have a history of overworking yourself, so you've been outright ban ned ( ばん ) from showing up at night . Hints Stop working so much! Humans need some rest too, so it can't always be bright. Maybe you should try some therapy. We all just want to see you get better, sun. Anyway, you're banned for now. Cya.

meaningMnemonic: A giant shrimp appears on top of the sun after it rises high above the ground , and this is how you know it's noon . The shrimp appears on the sun exactly at noon every day, to announce that it's noon. Hints Really try to imagine this giant shrimp on the sun as a normal thing that happens, without fail, every day at noon. "Hey guys, it's noon," the shrimp announces casually, then leaves again.
readingMnemonic: At noon , the shrimp also puts on its high heel s ( ひる ). It wants to look good for the other shrimp it's going to lunch with. High noon? More like high heels, am I right? Hints Right after the shrimp's noon announcement, imagine it struggling to put on heels while sitting on the sun. This shrimp is almost bigger than the sun, actually, so all its heel struggles are easy to see.

meaningMnemonic: Your fingers are private , no one can see them unless they pay ! And you decide if what they pay is enough to get a peek. Hints Imagine people coming from miles around to pay for a look at your private fingers.
readingMnemonic: If someone tries to look without paying, that's hara ssment ( はら )! Nobody gets to see something of yours without proper payment, but more importantly, your consent! Hints If somebody looks at your fingers without paying, without your consent, file a harassment claim on their butt! That is NOT okay!

meaningMnemonic: A rib cage hanging in the window of a shop indicates they sell poison . It's a universal sign, kinda like barber poles or those crosses on pharmacies. Hints Sure, it's pretty graphic, but most poison vendors don't want you wandering in unless you really mean business.
readingMnemonic: Ask any poison vendor: the middle of a Su doku ( どく ) puzzle is the best time to poison someone. They'll be concentrating so hard on their Sudoku puzzle that they won't even notice the poison begin to set in… until it's too late. Hints Imagine walking up to the register at your local poison shop with a couple vials of poison and a stack of Sudoku booklets. The cashier gives you a knowing nod and says, "You really know your stuff, huh?"

meaningMnemonic: Once the sun comes out, you can use this key to unlock it and take you to any previous day, even just yesterday ! The sun is in charge of the day changes, so if you use a key to unlock it, you can control the flow of time and return to yesterday, or a previous day in the past. Behold the power of the sun. Hints Imagine having the power to control time like this. Picture yourself unlocking the sun to go back in time. Feel the heat of the sun and the bright light in your eyes as you unlock the door to the past.
readingMnemonic: Time traveling to a previous time, like yesterday , can be rough on the body. As such, you wear a small sack ( さく ) to hold your valuables while you're ripped through the sands of time. The sack keeps your important stuff from getting lost. The sack holds your key to the sun as well. Hints Imagine wearing this sack as you're sucked through the vortex of time and space. Feel yourself spinning around as you hurtle back into yesterday.

meaningMnemonic: You pick up your knife and broom because you're getting ready to return home . There'll be a lot of work to do when you return home — cooking, cleaning, fixing stuff — so your knife and broom are sure to come in handy. Hints Your knife is one of those Swiss Army knives, so it's got a bunch of tools you'll need when you return home. Your broom is just a broom, but… maybe if you pretend to ride it like a witch, it'll make the trip home more fun?
readingMnemonic: For you to return home , your family has to ask the world to 返 す ( かえ ) you to them. You belong at home with your family — the outside world is just borrowing you, and eventually it needs to 返す you and let you return home. Hints Imagine your family asking all your coworkers and friends to 返す you so you can return home. It's heartwarming, but also kind of embarrassing at the same time.

meaningMnemonic: A good ceremony is under construction for a long time. You can't just make up a new ceremony on the spot. A ceremony is done a certain way because that's the way it's always been done. In short, to build a ceremony, you have to create a ritual first. Then, the ritual can be constructed into a bigger, more lavish ceremony . This kanji also means equation for some reason. Just think of a ceremony that involves doing math and solving equations. How strange would that be? Pretend you're at this ceremony. Hints Ritual and ceremony kind of mean the same thing. Don't worry too much if you mix them up a little — each will help you to remember the other. There's a reason this kanji is made up of the ceremony radical already!
readingMnemonic: So, you're at a ritual , but not just any old ritual. This is a full-blown ceremony and it's incredibly chic ( しき ). Imagine just how chic it is. Give it a shot — I'll let you come up with the chicness this time (it's good practice). Hints It's good to practice making up your own mnemonics every once in a while. It'll help if you add more to the mnemonics already here, or if you can make up new ones that are more personal to you!

meaningMnemonic: Take your yakuza knife and put it in a row with the others. Hints You have a yakuza knife. There are a bunch there, all in a row, so you follow suit by putting yours in the row too.
readingMnemonic: Should we put them in a row ? Let's ( れつ ) put them in a row! Hints Imagine a bunch of yakuza being enthusiastic about putting their knives in a row. They all say together "Ret's do it!"

meaningMnemonic: After a tsunami , if you go to a bar , you'll find yourself standing in shallow water. You're just trying to enjoy a drink, but with your feet constantly soaked, it's not exactly pleasant. Here's to hoping the conversations with your date won't be shallow too! Hints Picture yourself at this bar, sipping on a drink while you're wading in this shallow water. Feel the shallow water getting your socks and shoes all wet. It's uncomfortable and cold.
readingMnemonic: What beer are you drinking at this bar while standing in shallow water? You’re drinking Asa hi ( あさ ), the beer of the salaryman. Asahi is super dry, so it takes your attention away from the shallow water a bit. Hints Picture yourself in the bar again sipping on this Asahi beer. Taste the beery beer taste of Asahi as you walk around the bar with your wet feet.

meaningMnemonic: The simple radical and the simple kanji are the same! Hints Simple is simple!
readingMnemonic: One of the most simple things in the world is getting a tan ( たん ). All you have to do is stand outside long enough. It doesn't matter what skin type you have or what the weather is like. Eventually, if you stand out there long enough, you'll get a tan. Hints Get a tan, it's simple, stupid! (Though it's terrible for you so uh... don't always take our advice, kay?)

meaningMnemonic: You can make your fingers branch out. It's your special skill , a very advanced technique . Your fingers branch out into smaller fingers and you can hold things really well. You can type super-duper fast. And you can win any tickle fight. These are skills you have thanks to your branching fingers. Hints If you could have any skill imaginable, what would it be? Wouldn't it be nice to have these magical branching fingers? (Definitely. It would.)
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately, these skill s are too much for the normal skill-less people to handle, so they pull out the gui llotine ( ぎ ). I guess they're going to chop off your skillful fingers because they're kinda scary. Hints Imagine a tiny guillotine made for the cutting of fingers. Whoever made this must have had special hand skills too! Then maybe the skill-less people tested it on them…

meaningMnemonic: Dirt is being anti -social when it's in the shape of a slope . Think about it — is there anything more annoying than having to walk up a steep slope? Why is the dirt here forming a slope?! Because the dirt is being anti-social, and a slope is how it tells you to stay away. Hints Imagine the pain in your calves as you walk up a steep slope. Wow, this dirt is really anti-you right now. Going down the slope will be a lot easier and quicker, but that's still just the dirt trying to shoo you away as fast as possible.
readingMnemonic: You need to know these things about slope s if you want to play soccer ( さか ). Soccer is surprisingly slope-intensive, actually. Hints Maybe it looks flat to a spectator, but a soccer pitch is actually a series of very small slopes. Those soccer athletes who seem to fall and flop all the time are in fact just slipping on tiny invisible slopes.

meaningMnemonic: In the cage there are some legs . They are the legs attached to a small animal . Hints You can only see the legs, though, because a cloth is covering the cage. What kind of small animal is it? Try to look.
readingMnemonic: You look up through the cloth, and see a hairless cat. This small animal is hairless, but most surprisingly is covered in hickie s ( ひき ). Hints Who is giving this cat all those hickies? Pretty gross, if you ask me.

meaningMnemonic: When you see the spring sun you know it's finally the spring season. Hints The spring sun shows itself only in spring, and that's how you know the season has truly arrived. Its light has a special quality that gives everything a fresh, spring-like hue.
readingMnemonic: You also know spring has arrived when you start hallu cinating ( はる ). With all the funky pollens wafting around, it's kind of inevitable that spring will make you hallucinate — it's just part of the season. Hints Just picture how lively everything becomes in the springtime, and let yourself be guided by the wonderful sounds, smells and colours. Let yourself enjoy the hallucinations.

meaningMnemonic: This building has easy access to sunshine . The sunlight shines right in, because it's a clear building. Hints Feel the sunshine coming into the building. It gets into this building so easily, and makes it very bright and warm. No matter where you look, sunshine is everywhere.
readingMnemonic: The sunshine gets into the building so easily, in fact, that it hits your yo gurt ( よう ). The sunshine makes the yogurt... gross. Hints Picture your yogurt glistening in the sunlight. Watch as it slowly curdles and starts to smell sour. You still eat your yogurt, but it's hot and lumpy now. Sunlight and yogurt do not mix.

meaningMnemonic: There go some angel s with drop s on their shoulders. Carrying drops like that requires technique . It’s a real art . Hints Angels are really good at going around carrying drops! Imagine the artistry and technique involved. I bet they do some kind of dance, and there's lots of sparkly magic.
readingMnemonic: Angels are so good at this because they are trained in nin jutsu ( じゅつ ), or the "ninja techniques." Everyone knows that ninjas are great at carrying drops on the go! Hints Imagine an angel trained in ninjutsu. Marvel at all their divine ninja techniques!

meaningMnemonic: The temple radical and the temple kanji are exactly the same! Brilliant.
readingMnemonic: Someone died. You ask how this person died, the person who's getting buried by the temple . The priest/monk says it was in a tragic terror ( てら ) attack. Hints That's too bad - feel sorry for the person and learn a little more about the terror attack, if it will help you to remember the reading of this kanji better.

meaningMnemonic: Drink ing as much as you want is nice and all, but don't get sick. When you see this word, you know you're at an all you can drink place. Tip: Usually there's a time limit, so drink up!
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the word 放題 ( ほうだい ) and 飲む ( のむ ). So long as you know those vocab words, you'll be able to read this one as well.

meaningMnemonic: A strange person is an eccentric . They are also an oddball .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: The noun form of request (don't be tricked by the い on the end, it's not an adjective). So, request goes to a request .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same like お願いします . Hopefully you're able to read that by now so you're able to read this too.

a request of a lifetime, an extremely important request

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

sentences.english: He decided to join the military.

meaningMnemonic: An occurrence that causes change somehow can also be called an incident . 事変 is a formal word for big, unexpected incidents that are disruptive and chaotic. This can involve natural disasters, sudden riots, or other large-scale disturbances that need military intervention. It can also refer to unannounced warfare. You'll most likely see this word used in names for historical events, like the Manshuu Jihen ( 満州事変 ), or the Manchurian Incident. The 変 kanji suggests "change," so you know 事変 is only used for historical incidents big enough to make things change!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: When you see someone doubting you and return something successful instead, that is to show someone what one can do or more simply to show someone . In other words, you show someone who doubted you or treated you unfairly what you’re really capable of. There are a couple of other meanings, too. It can mean to look back over something , like the answers to your kanji test you want to double check, and sometimes to return someone’s stare . You can see how all of these meanings relate to the kanji, right?
readingMnemonic: The readings are from the words 見 and 返す put together.

meaningMnemonic: The simple bits of language are the individual word s. If you think about it, this is true. First of all, there are a ton of them. Second, they're tiny.
